clinicalPearls: Results from haploinsufficiency of EFTUD2, which encodes a GTPase subunit of the U5 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein within the major spliceosome, placing the condition among the spliceosomopathies rather than the classic chromatin disorders

The cardinal combination is malar and mandibular hypoplasia together with progressive microcephaly, which helps separate it from Treacher Collins syndrome where head circumference is usually preserved
External ear anomalies such as microtia and atresia of the external auditory canal are common and frequently accompanied by conductive hearing loss requiring early audiological input
Oesophageal atresia with or without tracheo-oesophageal fistula and choanal atresia are recognised associations that may declare themselves in the neonatal period
Supporting features include cleft palate, congenital heart defects, thumb and radial ray anomalies, epibulbar dermoids and clefts of the zygomatic arch
Developmental delay and intellectual disability of variable degree are usual, so neurodevelopmental follow-up should be arranged from infancy
Diagnosis is confirmed by finding a heterozygous, usually de novo, loss-of-function EFTUD2 variant or a 17q21.31 deletion encompassing the gene
reference.pathophysiology: EFTUD2 encodes a conserved GTPase that forms part of the U5 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein of the major spliceosome, the molecular machine that removes introns from pre-messenger RNA. Loss-of-function variants reduce the amount of functional protein (haploinsufficiency), impairing efficient and accurate splicing during a critical window of embryonic development. Tissues derived from the neural crest, which give rise to much of the facial skeleton and ears, appear particularly sensitive to this reduction, producing the characteristic mandibulofacial dysostosis. Concurrent disturbance of neuronal proliferation is thought to underlie the microcephaly and intellectual disability, while disrupted patterning of the foregut and other structures accounts for the oesophageal and cardiac anomalies.
additionalDifferentials: Nager acrofacial dysostosis (SF3B4, a related spliceosomopathy)
additionalInvestigations: Exome or genome sequencing to detect EFTUD2 sequence variants, including small intragenic deletions
Chromosomal microarray to identify 17q21.31 deletions that encompass EFTUD2
Formal audiological assessment with temporal bone imaging where hearing loss is suspected
Neonatal evaluation for oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula when feeding difficulty or excess secretions occur
Echocardiography to screen for congenital heart disease
Brain MRI to characterise structural anomalies underlying the microcephaly
Ophthalmological review for epibulbar dermoids and assessment of choanal patency
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory distress or choking on feeds suggesting choanal atresia or oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula
Upper airway obstruction from severe mandibular hypoplasia and glossoptosis
Unrecognised conductive hearing loss compromising early language acquisition
reference.prognosis: Outcome is highly variable and is driven chiefly by the severity of airway compromise, feeding difficulty and cardiac disease in infancy; with coordinated multidisciplinary care these can often be managed, after which intellectual ability determines longer-term function across a wide spectrum from mild to severe impairment.
pitfalls: Labelling the child as Treacher Collins syndrome and thereby overlooking the microcephaly and intellectual disability that point to EFTUD2
Failing to look for oesophageal atresia or tracheo-oesophageal fistula in a neonate with excessive secretions
Delaying audiological assessment so that treatable conductive hearing loss impairs speech development
Assuming a normal karyotype excludes the diagnosis when microdeletion and single-gene testing are required
references: Nature Reviews Genetics — spliceosomopathies and craniofacial development
